title: On-Prem Decision Tree + Skepticisms Messaging
content:
Purpose:
This is a short, practical playbook intended for sellers and solutions engineers who are engaging regulated buyers (healthcare, finserv, gov) about private deployments (VPC / on-prem). Focus: an easy-to-follow decision tree, succinct control-plane language that reduces legal & security friction, and concise rebuttals for the common skepticisms we see early in the cycle.

How to use this doc (quick):
- If buyer is worried about data egress, start with 'control-plane locality' section.
- If procurement brings up 'liability / model outputs', use the 'model governance + audit' snippets.
- If SRE or infra asks about upgrades/patching window, run the 'ops modes' script and pilot ask.

Executive framing (single-sentence anchors sellers can use):
- "We give you the same developer API you know, with control and telemetry that stays inside your network — so you get model velocity without changing your security boundaries."
- "Redwood Private separates orchestration metadata (control plane) from customer data and runtime — you choose where the control plane lives."

Decision tree (high level):
- Does the customer require data never leave their VPC or on-prem?
  - Yes -> Recommend Private (air-gapped option if required). Focus: on-prem runtime + customer-managed KMS, local telemetry sinks.
  - No -> Are they comfortable with a customer-hosted control plane in their cloud account?
    - Yes -> Private (VPC control plane) with customer-owned control-plane resources and explicit SLA mappings.
    - No, but want vendor-managed control plane -> Offer Dedicated with strict contract clauses and optional regional isolation.

Buyer personas & primary concerns (elevator notes):
- CISO (risk-focused): data residency, keys, auditability, breach blast radius.
- Platform/Cloud Infra (ops-focused): upgrade windows, image provenance, observability hooks, automation integration (Terraform, Helm).
- App Product Lead (developer-focused): SDK parity, latency, model rollouts, cost predictability.
- Procurement/Legal: indemnities, data processor vs controller language, SLAs and termination data handling.

Concise control-plane language (use these exact lines where possible):
- "Control plane metadata (task scheduling, instance lifecycle) is configuration data — it contains no customer PII or model output. Customers can host the control plane in their account or use a narrow vendor-managed endpoint with IP allowlists."
- "Runtime that touches customer requests (model inference, KV caches, logs with sensitive tokens) always runs in customer-owned compute unless an explicit opt-in is accepted."
- "Keys and secrets remain under customer KMS/HSM — Redwood never has access to plaintext customer keys in private deployments."

Competitive positioning & quick notes (call-outs sellers should memorize):
- Competitor A: heavy-weight on-prem bundles; long lead times for upgrades and opaque kernel changes. Our angle: lightweight runtime images, automated patch bundles, documented upgrade path with rollback.
- Competitor B: promises control but centralizes telemetry ingest. Our angle: telemetry optionality — bring-your-own log sinks (S3, GCS, Splunk, local SIEM) and sampling controls.
- Open-source runtimes: attractive on cost but require infra expertise to maintain complex batching/caching and to reach production latency SLOs. Our angle: we manage the inference economics and provide tuning guidance and instrumentation out of the box.

Common buyer objections + tight rebuttals (short script + evidence to move forward):
- Objection: "If you control the control plane, you can see our prompts — we won't allow it."
  - Script: "We can run the control plane in your account or provide a minimal vendor-managed endpoint that handles only scheduling tokens (no request payload). We also support mutual-TLS and IP allowlists; we can demonstrate the control-plane AMI/Helm chart in a proof-of-concept."
  - Evidence to offer: architecture diagram, temporary read-only access to audit logs, model of data flow with redaction markers.
- Objection: "How do you guarantee model outputs won't leak regulated info?"
  - Script: "We provide workload isolation, model version pinning, and a built-in audit trail for prompts/outputs. For very sensitive workloads, we recommend inference within an on-prem enclave and application-layer redaction rules."
  - Evidence: sample audit export, compliance checklist for PHI/PII, pointer to our 'quality monitoring' eval suite.
- Objection: "Upgrades will break us — we can't risk downtime."
  - Script: "Upgrades are staged via canaries and A/B rollouts; we provide an opt-in 'frozen' channel for production-critical clusters while still shipping security patches as signed backports."
  - Evidence: release cadence doc, rollback runbook, SLOs for upgrade windows.

Pilot ask & negotiation levers (practical, short):
- Starter pilot: 2-node private runtime in customer account (2 GPUs or equiv) + 2-week embed/latency bench + access to rollbacks. Pilot ask: engineering contact, infra admin seat, legal 'pilot MSA' with limited liability for 90 days.
- Data-proof pilot: red-team prompt set and reconstructed audit trail to demonstrate no egress. Ask minimal set of sample prompts (anonymized).
- Concessions we can make (fast wins): discounted pilot rate, extended log retention for audit period, time-limited code escrow for custom connectors.

Operational modes (how customers typically run):
- Customer-hosted control plane: preferred for largest regulated buyers. Pros: max auditability and KMS control. Cons: requires buyer infra work.
- Vendor-managed control plane in customer region: fast to onboard; we minimize surface area (only scheduling/metadata). Good middle ground.
- Fully on-prem airgapped: reserved for top tier financial and defense customers. Requires signed contracts and devops runbook; plan 6–12 week lead.

Playbook for first 90 minutes of a buyer call (cheat-sheet for AE/SE):
1) 0–4m: Quick intro; one-line about control-plane locality and where keys live.
2) 4–12m: Ask persona-specific questions (CISO: "Which logs must remain on-prem?").
3) 12–20m: Show two slides: a) data flow (control plane variants) b) pilot outline and timeline.
4) 20–30m: Cover top 3 objections with the short scripts above. Ask for next steps: pilot commitment or tech deep-dive.

Unresolved / open questions (notes for product/engineering follow-up):
- Need a concise diagram pack that explicitly labels 'no-PII' boundaries for the control plane vs runtime.
- Can we produce a pre-approved legal clause library (data residency + KMS attestation) that sales can attach to SOWs?
- Clarify support model for BYO KMS across cloud vendors (edge cases for on-prem HSM integrations).

Short email template (for SE -> CISO follow-up):
Subject: Demo assets + pilot plan (private deployment)
Hi [CISO Name],
Thanks again for the conversation. As discussed, attached are: 1) two-page architecture note showing how control plane metadata is separated from inference payloads; 2) a 2-week pilot outline that runs in your account with telemetry directed to your SIEM; 3) our pilot MSA summary.
If you like, I can schedule a 30-min walkthrough with our infra engineer to map the integration points.
Best,
[SE name]

Next steps (internal):
- Create the OMG (one-minute guide) diagram for each control-plane mode. [Owner: Jonah, due 2025-03-12]
- Draft legal clause pack for pilot MSA. [Owner: Lena, due 2025-03-20]
- Build a quick demo harness that shows telemetry being routed to Splunk/GCS. [Owner: Samir, due 2025-03-18]

Notes to self (informal):
- Keep messaging simple: 'where control plane runs' + 'who owns keys' = 80% of objections.
- Avoid saying 'we never see data' — better to say 'we do not have access to plaintext keys or customer-managed storage without explicit contract-level consent.'
- Save detailed infra diagrams for the tech deep-dive; the CISO wants the high-level boundary first.

End of doc.
